title: Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard -- Ch. 10: Civil Servants' Right to Compensation During Preventive Suspension
keywords: Civil Servants' Right to Compensation During Preventive Suspension
primary_topics: Chapter 10 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' -- CJP's argument that a civil servant who is eventually exonerated must be paid back salaries for BOTH kinds of preventive suspension, pending appeal and pending investigation, and his hope that the Supreme Court will one day reverse Gloria v. Court of Appeals insofar as it denied back pay for the investigation period

An exposition of the two kinds of preventive suspension under the present Civil Service Law (Book V, Title I, Subtitle A of the Administrative Code of 1987, EO 292): suspension pending investigation under Sec. 51, capped at ninety days with automatic reinstatement under Sec. 52, and suspension pending appeal under Sec. 47, par. 4

A critique of the Gloria majority's method: its heavy reliance on the construction rule that 'amendment by deletion' of the old RA 2260 phrase 'full pay for the period of suspension' signals a change of legislative meaning, and its borrowing from Mechem the requirement that a suspension be not only followed by exoneration but also 'unjustified'

His reproduction of his own Separate Opinion, arguing that withholding an exonerated employee's pay converts a non-penal preventive suspension into an unauthorized penalty that violates due process, and that the constitutional command to 'afford full protection to labor' must resolve any doubt in the employee's favor
sub_topics: He opens by quoting the present Civil Service Law in full -- Secs. 47, 51 and 52 of Book V, Title I, Subtitle A of the Administrative Code of 1987 (EO 292) -- as the governing text
He distills from those provisions the two kinds of preventive suspension: pending investigation (Sec. 51) and pending appeal where the respondent is later exonerated (Sec. 47, par. 4)

He restates the practical scheme: immediate 90-day suspension to keep respondents from intimidating or influencing witnesses, automatic reinstatement if the investigation is unfinished, continued suspension during appeal, and compensation if eventually exonerated

He reports the holding of Gloria v. Court of Appeals, where a divided Court, through Justice Vicente V. Mendoza, allowed compensation only for the suspension pending appeal and not for the days pending investigation

He identifies the majority's two supports: the deletion from EO 292 of RA 2260's express grant of 'full pay for the period of suspension,' and Mechem's rule that exoneration is not enough because the suspension must also be 'unjustified'

He recalls that during the Court's deliberations he argued for back wages covering the investigation period too, calling the Court too literal and unfair and warning that the strict construction rule effectively reversed earlier rulings awarding back salaries 'without any qualification or deduction'

He quotes his Separate Opinion: since the majority concedes preventive suspension pending investigation is not a penalty but only an investigative device, withholding pay would transform it into a penalty unauthorized by law and unconstitutional for want of due process

He rejects 'no-work-no-pay' for suspended employees, who are willing to work but are barred from reporting, may go three months without salary, and may face baseless charges -- making their suspensions unjustified ab initio

He answers the deletion argument: the silence of EO 292 is not a denial of the right, construction rules are only tools for finding legislative intent, and EO 292 -- issued by President Corazon Aquino under the Freedom Constitution -- has no recorded deliberations from which intent can be verified

He invokes the Constitution above any treatise, including Mechem's: the fundamental law's mandate to 'afford full protection to labor' and to 'protect the rights of workers and promote their welfare' has no counterpart in the United States Constitution and covers civil servants as part of the working class
He frames back pay as justice and equity rather than compassion, warning that denial opens the door to harassment and oppression of innocent public servants and their families
He draws the private-sector comparison: unjustly dismissed private employees get reinstatement without loss of seniority plus full back wages and allowances

He distinguishes the Civil Service Law from the Ombudsman Act (RA 6770), whose Sec. 24 expressly makes preventive suspension run 'without pay' -- the reason no back pay was awarded in Callanta v. Ombudsman
He closes with the hope that the Court will reverse Gloria, insisting the government should set the example in giving labor its due before preaching labor-law compliance to private employers
signature_phrases: the Court was being too literal and unfair to government employees
The 'no-work-no-pay' principle should not be applied in these cases
their suspensions are unjustified ab initio
a penalty which is unauthorized by law
in the absence of an express prohibition on the payment of back salaries, any doubt should be settled in favor of the employee
It is my fervent hope that one day soon, the Supreme Court will reverse Gloria
Only then can it be sanctimonious in its directives to private employers to observe labor laws.

stances.claim: A civil servant who is eventually exonerated should be paid back wages not only for the preventive suspension pending appeal but also for the days of preventive suspension pending investigation, because in that case the suspension was unjustified from the start.
stances.rhetorical_move: equity-and-fairness argument built on the exoneration itself: if there was no offense, there was no reason to deprive the employee of work and income

stances.claim: Because the majority concedes that preventive suspension pending investigation is not a penalty but only a device for an unhampered investigation, withholding an exonerated employee's salary for that period transforms it into a penalty unauthorized by law, contrary to due process and therefore unconstitutional.
stances.rhetorical_move: turning the majority's own premise against its conclusion, then escalating from statutory to constitutional ground

stances.claim: The rule on 'amendment by deletion' cannot control here, since construction rules are mere tools for ascertaining legislative intent and EO 292 -- issued under the Freedom Constitution -- has no recorded deliberations from which an intent to change the old law can be verified.
stances.rhetorical_move: methodological rebuttal: limiting a canon of construction to cases where the legislative intent to change is clear

stances.claim: Any doubt must be resolved for the employee because the Constitution commands full protection to labor, and civil servants are very much part of the working class -- with the government, as employer, obliged to set the example.
stances.rhetorical_move: constitutional hierarchy plus private-sector parity: the fundamental law outranks a foreign treatise, and public employees should not get less than private ones

notable_anecdotes: He recalls arguing during the Court's own deliberations in Gloria for back wages covering the investigation period, and losing to a divided majority.
He reproduces long passages of his Separate Opinion in Gloria, letting the dissenting argument speak in its original judicial voice.

He notes that the ponencia leaned on Mechem, a foreign treatise, and answers that 'our Constitution stands above all laws' and that the United States Constitution contains no comparable labor-protection mandate.
He points out that EO 292 was issued by President Corazon Aquino under the Freedom Constitution and has no recorded deliberations -- so its legislative purpose simply cannot be established.
He contrasts Callanta v. Ombudsman, where petitioners merely reprimanded still received no back pay, because the Ombudsman Act expressly makes preventive suspension run without pay.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 10 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' set out CJP's position that an exonerated civil servant is entitled to back salaries for every day of preventive suspension, including the period pending investigation. He began by quoting the present Civil Service Law -- Secs. 47, 51 and 52 of Book V, Title I, Subtitle A of the Administrative Code of 1987 (EO 292) -- and distilled from it two kinds of preventive suspension: suspension pending investigation, which runs up to ninety days and ends in automatic reinstatement if the case is not decided, and suspension pending appeal, which entitles the respondent to compensation if he is eventually exonerated. He then reported Gloria v. Court of Appeals, where a divided Court speaking through Justice Vicente V. Mendoza allowed pay only for the appeal period, reasoning that EO 292 had deleted the old RA 2260 grant of 'full pay for the period of suspension' and that, per Mechem, exoneration is not enough because the suspension must also have been 'unjustified.' CJP recounted arguing the contrary in the Court's deliberations -- that the majority was being too literal and unfair to government employees and was in effect reversing earlier rulings awarding back salaries 'without any qualification or deduction' -- and reproduced his Separate Opinion. There he argued that since the majority itself conceded that preventive suspension pending investigation is not a penalty but only a means to an unhampered investigation, withholding pay would transform it into a penalty unauthorized by law and offensive to due process; that 'no-work-no-pay' cannot apply to employees who are willing to work but forbidden to report; that baseless charges make a suspension unjustified ab initio; that the silence of EO 292, a law issued by President Corazon Aquino under the Freedom Constitution with no recorded deliberations, cannot be read as a denial of the right; and that the constitutional mandate to afford full protection to labor, which has no United States counterpart, resolves any doubt for the employee. He distinguished the Ombudsman Act, which expressly makes suspension run without pay, as in Callanta v. Ombudsman, and closed by hoping the Court would reverse Gloria so that government could set the example in giving labor its due.
